window_text:
[9] Kevin: You guys have met our friend the erg over here?
[10] Charles: Yeah. Yeah of course.
[11] Jillian: Of course.
[12] Kevin: Well cool. My name is Kevin Allen, I’m the CEO of Row Vigor. And this is Moses, he is our Chief Technology Officer. So about three years ago, a good friend of mine I’ve known since I was 13 years old, 20 year fitness professional, came to me and he said - I think there’s an opportunity for rowing based fitness in our space. He said, he kept having customers that come to him asking for good rowing based fitness.
So Kevin did some research — and he discovered that rowing is actually a very effective way to workout. It’s a low-impact exercise that works 85% of your muscle groups.
[13] Kevin: I found out a lot of good things about rowing and rowing fitness in general that spelled opportunity for me. a lot of physical therapists recommend rowing, particularly when you have a knee or hip replacement. I found out that there wasn’t really a big national brand for rowing based fitness.
So Kevin and his friend set out to see if they could be the ones, to start that first, rowing-based fitness brand.
In August 2016 ROWViGOR was born. They set up a pop-up rowing studio in the D.C. area with the goal of getting 1000 people to join.
[14] Kevin: We wanted to build a community around rowing based fitness. Seven months later we had our thousand people. We had been written up in The Washington Post, we were rated one of the top fitness experiences in the area
Over time, they refined their business model, choosing to go after a much larger market than a brick-and-mortar gym:
at-home fitness
. Essentially, they want to bring rowing right to people’s homes through a bluetooth-enabled rowing machine.
Kevin and Moses are valuing their company at 3 million dollars and are here today to raise the 500 thousand dollars they need to get their product off the ground.
[15] Kevin: 
Fast forward to today. I think the timing is right for software that can support rowing based fitness and a community based experience at home. and now we’re 30 days from launching our in-home product that we call the Vigor Box. The Vigor Box is everything you need to enjoyrowing based fitness./
In addition the rowing machine, the Vigor Box will include access to a library of rowing classes.
[16] Kevin: would you like to see one? We can show you one of our classes.
[17] Jillian: Yeah.
[18] Moses: We made our app both for iPad as well as the iPhone.
This is Moses, Kevin’s cofounder.
[19] Moses: What we did with our brick and mortar, we looked at our most popular classes, and we basically took the data from that and we selected our top three classes from that. And so here's our fitness partner, Fola.
Moses presses play on one of the classes available in the ROWVIGOR app.
[music]
[20] Jillian: Oh I like this.
[21] Fola: Shoulders stay back the entire time.
[22] Jillian: I don't know if I like him or this.
[23] Moses: Either way. Either way.
On the screen the instructor, Fola, is walking viewers through a popular rowing routine so they can follow along at home. It’s worth noting that, unlike a lot of the current fitness trends, ROWViGOR is going old school with these pre-recorded classes.
[24] Phil: So there won't be live classes that the rowers participate in?
[25] Kevin: No. In the beginning there will be archive classes. Could we go to a live class model? Absolutely. Could we go to a model where we set up cameras inside various studios and strike deals with different brick and mortar based companies? Absolutely. Right now we're hyper focused on an archive based solution on the training, on the goal setting. But these are all possibilities for us down the line.
[26] Jillian: So Phil you're a big Peloton person. Correct?
[27] Phil: I like their business model a lot. I don't have one.
[28] Jillian: Oh, I thought you had one.
[29] Phil: No. I think a lot of people who, friends of mine who use Peloton and they say two things about the live classes they like. One is that they see that leaderboard and they see themselves competing and how they’re doing on the leaderboard. And the other is that they get shout outs from the instructor, from the leader, who says, come on Jillian! Pick it up! You’re in 32nd place. Come on, you can do it. And they actually get that motivation real time live for them.
This competition element that Phil is talking about is at the heart of a lot of the current blockbuster fitness brands, including Peloton and CrossFit. While they certainly have their differences — CrossFit is a brick-and-mortar gym while Peloton is home-based fitness — they both have this one important thing in common: live classes that promote a sense of community among their members.
But Kevin thinks those brands are missing out on an even bigger opportunity.
[30] Kevin: One of the things we see in the fitness market is that a lot of people are putting content out. Which Peloton is doing in an outstanding way. But they're not supporting their customers in a journey. I was talking to a woman the other day who has a Peloton bike and she said, I love it, I love the classes. But what I don't love is that there's no accountability. No one is telling me that I have to go to class. No one is asking about me if I don't join that class.
[31] ROWViGOR has found a way to unlock that accountability piece: by connecting each member with a personal trainer - the trainer will work with members to make sure they’re hitting their fitness goals.
[32] Kevin: Somebody is there looking at your data saying, hey, Kevin, you've only been on the erg once this week. You have a goal in six months to be ready for your daughter's wedding. Why aren't you getting on the erg? So we make everybody give us a goal, we onboard them that way, and we continually refine those goals.
[33] Charles: How specific does a goal have to be? Because I'd imagine a lot of people are like, I just want to get in shape. It's not a specific, it's not tied to an event, it's not tied to a specific weight loss goal, I just want to get in shape. That's one. And two, what is retention, what does retention have to look like for a service like this for it to make sense for you?
[34] Kevin: We want to be north of 85% in terms of keeping people engaged. We think we can do better than that. We're looking at this in the 90 - 95% range just because of the elements that we talked about.
[35] Daniel: That would be insanely phenomenal.
[36] Phil: Off the charts.
[37] Charles: For your category. That would be a whole other world.
[38] Kevin: But, you know, we also believe that in terms of goal setting, you can make it as specific as you want to make it. We would want the person, and the reason, we have a very specific process laid out that includes you setting a goal first, which may be very general, and then us following up and asking you a question or two. That's that personal training piece, and that's why that's so important.
And the personal trainer does more than just help you set goals.
[39] Kevin: First of all, we do teach the right rowing technique. On the app, all the time, is somebody showing you the proper rowing technique. Second of all, because we allowed basically Facetime for Row Vigor, you can actually plug in, show a trainer, this is how I'm rowing, and they can correct you real time through the application.
[40] Daniel: I actually really like the hybrid model that you guys are going for. The personal trainer plus the content library. And how does content creation work? How does that piece of the puzzle fit? So at the moment it sounds like you guys are developing your own programs, developing this your own content, essentially, on the app.What's that piece?
[41] Kevin: So early on, we're going to replicate what has been successful for us to date, and that's filming existing classes, basically staged classes. So like you might see, going back to the old Jane Fonda workouts.
[42] Jillian: I love those! I still have that by the way. On the tape. I'm not kidding you.
[43] Kevin: They're great. They're great.
[44] Jillian: I still have the machine, because I can't get it on a disc. I kid you not. I even have those little workout things on. You know, the leggings. They're sexy, aren't they? They smack sexy.
[45] Charles: Those are coming back aren’t they? I feel like they’re coming back.
[46] Jillian: Absolutely.
[47] Kevin: I could see that. That's a little scary in my mind.
[48] Jillian: Unbelievable.
[49] Kevin: You've done it a lot of times. My wife does our kettlebell workout every day. Like that's her thing.
[50] Jillian: Really? So the kettle bell. Okay, go back to the thing and then we'll ask you.
[51] Kevin: Filming existing workout staged. So not going into a class and filming a live class. Getting it staged. Running about $15 - 20,000 per production. We're working to get that cost down with our producer.
[52] Phil: How many do you have in the can?
[53] Kevin: We have three archived now.
[54] Daniel: And that's your own...
[55] Kevin: That's our own Row Vigor content.
Kevin’s trying to sell investors on the fact that ROWViGOR is on its way to building a huge library of high production classes. But is high production really a selling point for people?
[56] Daniel: When I think about media like that, I think a lot about substitutable media. Like, I go on YouTube, I find something that's like not as high production value, but I can probably find like a hundred videos on how to row the right way. is this content so much better than the free substitutes out there that folks would be willing to pay? And I get that there's a community element too, so I'm not just anchoring on the content. But have you seen any proof points around willingness to pay for a library of that high production value content?
[57] Kevin: Well, there's plenty of models out there where people are streaming content and getting paid for it.
[58] Daniel: and then how much is the consumer paying for the annual subscription?
[59] Phil: First for the Vigor Box what are they paying?
[60] Kevin: For the Vigor Box with the Concept 2 and a year's worth of subscription it's about $1400.
[61] Daniel: But just... So if I renew my subscription in year two, how much am I paying?
[62] Kevin: It'll be $25 a month right now on average. We're looking at a tiered strategy where we're giving users access to content based on that pricing.
[63] Phil: So the $25 a month includes how much?
[64] Kevin: $25 a month will include 30 minutes of personal training per month. And get you access to all of our content as it stands today.
For every question, Kevin has an answer. But the investors aren’t showing their cards, and it’s hard to tell if they think the Vigor Box is the next
it
thing in fitness.
[65] Daniel: Does the consumer want this bundle? So I could go out and get a rowing machine, I could go out and subscribe to MoveWith, I can go out and get a personal trainer. And that costs me x dollars, and that's an unbundled solution. This is a bundled solution. Why am I going for your bundle?
[66] Kevin: Convenience, mostly. Rowing is probably new to a lot of people in our consumer base, so they're saying I need a solution where somebody is going to support me in being successful at what I do. That's why we believe that people will come to us and want the whole bundle.It's not about just throwing content at you. It's aboutmaking you successful as a fitness person, as somebody who wants to have a healthy lifestyle.
[67] Daniel: I guess my point was I can still get that in a piecemeal way outside of Row Vigor.
[68] Kevin: It's a convenience play, quite honestly.
[69] Daniel: Is it a price play?
[70] Kevin: Um.
[71] Daniel: Because that would be compelling, if it was.
[72] Kevin: The personal training piece is certainly a price play. Because if you're going to get somebody personally, it could cost you $100, $150, $200 an hour or up. Because we're doing this virtually, we can offer it at a much reduced pricing point. So there is some value to that.
[73] Charles: But to Daniel’s point, can I unbundle if my gym has a rowing machine and I’m just looking to augment my workout? I like the instruction, I like Fola, I like the experience, but I don’t want to buy a Row Vigor for my house. Can I just, so you can have a headless subscription?
[74] Kevin: We have an app-only model as well built into this. So you can buy the app, you can buy the bundle. You can buy this in whatever pieces that you want.
So that changes things a bit, you don’t have to spend $1400 dollars with ROWViGOR, you could buy your rowing machine elsewhere, or if you’re one of those hardcore fitness people with your own personal erg, you can still use the ROWViGOR app a la cart, starting at $25 a month.
But even with this kind of flexibility, it remains to be seen if it’ll be enough to get people to change their fitness routine.
[75] Phil: So where are you in terms of traction? Where are you with revenue? What stage are you at? I don’t have a sense of that.
[76] Kevin: We’re 30 days away from launch. So we’ve got the application together, we’ve got, we’re polishing now, we’ve started pre-sales last week, just putting out, saying we’re going to have a Vigor Box, here’s what it looks like. Would you rent it or would you buy it? So we’re also starting to get indications of interest from there. But we are pre-revenue with regard to the product. We’ve made some money...
[77] Jillian: How much?
[78] Kevin: Excuse me?
[79] Jillian: How much have you made?
[80] Kevin: We made $40,000 during our little experiment in the brick and mortar. But again, that was designed to be an experiment. I don’t really consider that revenue because it’s not based on the model that we have. So we are pre-revenue technically. But we’re ready to go.
Kevin has made his case. Now it’s up to investors.
Here’s Phil
[81] Phil: Well, I think it’s a cool model. I like what you’re doing. Based on where you are today, it’s relatively simple because I feel like it’s too early. It’s pre-revenue. I don’t invest in pre-revenue companies. So those are some of my thoughts for why I’m passing.
Phil’s out, here’s Daniel

Phil’s out, here’s Daniel

taxonomy.label: business_model_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the startup’s revenue model, monetization approach, or service/automation mix as a driver of business viability.

taxonomy.label: business_viability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's concern that the overall business viability, model, or economics are not sufficiently compelling.

taxonomy.label: capital_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the startup will require substantial ongoing capital investment, increasing risk or misalignment with the investor’s funding capacity.

taxonomy.label: competitive_advantage_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s beliefs about what drives defensibility or sustainable competitive advantage in a market.

taxonomy.label: competitive_intensity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the category is highly competitive, attention‐constrained, and requires heavy marketing to win, reducing the likelihood of outsized success.

taxonomy.label: competitive_landscape_inertia
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the difficulty of displacing or changing behavior of incumbents due to entrenched solutions, habits, or workflows.

taxonomy.label: deal_terms_complexity_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the structure or details of deal terms (e.g., convertibles, SAFEs, preferred terms) may introduce complexity, ambiguity, or unfavorable outcomes.

taxonomy.label: decision_context_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints imposed by the specific evaluation format, environment, or context rather than the startup's fundamentals.

taxonomy.label: dilution_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the financing plan will cause excessive dilution relative to their ownership goals or stage fit.

taxonomy.label: execution_risk_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s concern that the team may not yet have demonstrated sufficient execution reliability or maturity for the risk level of the round.

taxonomy.label: founder_equity_incentive_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to ensuring founders retain sufficient ownership to remain properly motivated, aligned, and incentivized for the long-term company‐building journey.

taxonomy.label: founder_execution
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of the founders' execution ability, resourcefulness, pace, and operational grit.

taxonomy.label: founder_market_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales based on how well the founder's background, experience, or motivation aligns with the target market.

taxonomy.label: founder_qualities
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's perception of the founders' personal traits, capabilities, or appeal.

taxonomy.label: founder_skillset
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the founder's core skills or functional strengths relevant to company-building.

taxonomy.label: fund_economics_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor’s fund size, check size, or ownership goals that constrain how selective they must be when choosing investments.

taxonomy.label: fundraising_demand_signal
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the company will attract capital easily due to current or expected investor demand.

taxonomy.label: growth_projection_risk
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the company’s growth, revenue, or user‐scale projections are insufficiently modeled, unrealistic, or lack credible underlying assumptions.

taxonomy.label: investment_thesis_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's predefined investment thesis or mandate that restricts them to specific sectors, business models, or company types.

taxonomy.label: investment_upside_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's view that the risk‐reward profile offers disproportionately large potential returns relative to downside risk.

taxonomy.label: investor_domain_knowledge_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor lacking the necessary domain knowledge to effectively assess the technology, moat, competition, or overall viability of the opportunity.

taxonomy.label: investor_experience_bias
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's prior personal experiences, wins, losses, or operational history that shape their judgment of a new opportunity.

taxonomy.label: market_entry_path_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that there is a clear, reachable initial customer segment that can serve as an effective wedge into the larger market.

taxonomy.label: market_problem_validation
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the investor perceiving the underlying problem as real, important, or painful enough to support a venture-scale solution.

taxonomy.label: market_size_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s belief about the absolute or relative size and fluidity of the addressable market.

taxonomy.label: market_timing
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the timing is favorable or unfavorable for this market, category, or product to emerge or scale.

taxonomy.label: mission_alignment_preference
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's personal or emotional alignment with the startup's mission or purpose.

taxonomy.label: portfolio_conflict_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to constraints arising from existing portfolio investments that create competitive conflicts preventing a new investment.

taxonomy.label: product_adoption
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to evidence that end users are adopting and using the product meaningfully.

taxonomy.label: product_appeal_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s positive perception of the product’s appeal, quality, or desirability based on their own reaction.

taxonomy.label: product_differentiation_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to how unique, defensible, or hard-to-copy the product or technology is perceived to be.

taxonomy.label: product_success_factor_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to which product components or attributes are perceived as most essential to the startup's ability to succeed.

taxonomy.label: solution_feasibility_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor's belief that the proposed product or solution is technically or operationally feasible.

taxonomy.label: stage_valuation_mismatch
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception of a mismatch between the company’s stage of progress and the valuation being requested.

taxonomy.label: traction_repeatability_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that current traction, usage, or revenue signals are too early or insufficiently repeatable to support scaling.

taxonomy.label: unit_economics_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to the investor’s perception that the business benefits from structurally attractive unit economics, such as profitable or self-reinforcing customer acquisition.

taxonomy.label: venture_scale_concern
taxonomy.definition: Rationales related to concerns that the companys market dynamics, ceiling, or competitive landscape limit its ability to achieve venture-scale outcomes.

taxonomy.label: investor_value_add_fit
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the investor can contribute meaningful help, networks, or domain value beyond capital to this specific company.

taxonomy.label: founder_coachability_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how receptive the founder is to feedback, advice, or course-correction and their ability to read and respond to the room.

taxonomy.label: founder_communication_quality
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the founder's clarity, articulation, command of their numbers, and storytelling ability when presenting the business.

taxonomy.label: founder_motivation_authenticity
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about the genuineness, personal connection, or origin of the founder's drive to work on this particular problem.

taxonomy.label: go_to_market_strategy_assessment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about how the company will reach and acquire customers, including sales motion, channel scalability, and cost of acquisition.

taxonomy.label: founder_investor_vision_alignment
taxonomy.definition: Rationales about whether the founder's intended direction or focus for the company aligns with the path the investor believes in or would back.

taxonomy.label: corporate_structure_constraint
taxonomy.definition: Rationales tied to the company's legal entity, incorporation, jurisdiction, or IP-ownership structure as a barrier or condition to investing.
